_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Your YouTube picture is right for **one building block**. In our stack we use it a bit differently from “predict yes/no for the player.” Here is the exact role.

---

## What problem σ is solving

Once rosters exist, we need a number **L_C** = “how congested is *my* peer field?” for the **score**:

\[
S_i = A_i - \lambda L_C
\]

Congestion here means: **how many of my teammates count as serious, viable peers** — people good enough that you’re competing with them for attention, minutes, or (in the story) the scarce advancement slot.

The sigmoid is how we turn each teammate’s ability into a **peer-viability score** before averaging.

---

## Step-by-step method (one player *i*)

**Setup:** Player *i* is on a roster. Look at **teammates only** (leave-one-out: exclude *i*).

**Step 1 — For each teammate *j*, compute viability**

\[
v_j = \sigma\big(\gamma(A_j - \theta)\big) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\gamma(A_j - \theta)}}
\]

- **A_j** = teammate *j*’s ability  
- **θ** = viability cutline (“how good does a peer have to be to matter?”)  
- **γ** = sharpness (how binary vs gradual that judgment is)

Interpretation of **v_j**:

| Teammate ability | v_j (roughly) |
|------------------|---------------|
| A_j ≫ θ | ≈ 1 — “fully viable” peer |
| A_j = θ | **exactly 0.5** — on the fence |
| A_j ≪ θ | ≈ 0 — “doesn’t really count as competition” |

So your 0.5 rule applies **per teammate**: at A_j = θ, that peer is half-in, half-out. We do **not** apply a single 0.5 rule to “is player *i* selected?” — selection is **top-K by S_i**.

**Step 2 — Average over teammates (LOO)**

\[
L_C = \mathrm{mean}_{j \neq i}\, v_j = \mathrm{mean}_{j \neq i}\, \sigma(\gamma(A_j - \theta))
\]

- **L_C ≈ 0** — almost no viable peers around you  
- **L_C ≈ 1** — almost every teammate is a viable peer → **high congestion**

**Step 3 — Enter score**

\[
S_i = A_i - \lambda L_C
\]

High **L_C** **lowers** your score even if **A_i** is high — “talented, but buried among other viable players.”

**Step 4 — Select**  
Top **K** by **S_i** (deterministic in Phase B). Bins on the slides are just **readout** of where those selected players sit on pool mean.

That’s the full chain: **σ on each peer → average → subtract in score → rank → select.**

---

## Concrete mini-example

θ = 0.72, γ = 10, λ = 0.55. You have 3 teammates with abilities 0.90, 0.75, 0.50:

- j=1: A=0.90 → σ large (~0.85+) — viable  
- j=2: A=0.75 → σ ≈ 0.5+ — borderline viable  
- j=3: A=0.50 → σ small (~0.1) — not really viable  

**L_C** = mean of those three ≈ **0.5** (moderate congestion).  
If **A_i = 0.80**: **S_i ≈ 0.80 − 0.55×0.5 = 0.525**.

Same talent on a weak team (teammates all ~0.40) → **L_C ≈ 0** → **S_i ≈ 0.80**. Same **A_i**, different roster context → different rank.

---

## Why a sigmoid (and not just “count peers above θ”)?

The code actually has **both**:

```774:775:sports/tier1_pool_assignment.py
      pool_c_loo          — L_C hard: share of teammates with ability > θ  ∈ [0,1]
      pool_c_smooth_loo   — L_C soft: mean teammate σ(γ(A−θ))              ∈ [0,1]
```

**Phase B / Alex 539 track uses the smooth one** (`crowding_smooth`).

Reasons:

1. **Story:** “Viable peer” is not literally on/off — a teammate slightly above θ matters more than one far below. σ gives a **graded** contribution.
2. **Knobs:** **θ** moves the center of the step; **γ** moves from “fuzzy” to “almost hard threshold.” That’s what your θ and γ slides characterize.
3. **Math:** Smooth σ avoids a cliff at θ; λ_crit and sort-and-chop algebra use the logistic knee (memo 06: λ_crit ≈ 4/γ).

Hard version (count share with A_j > θ) is the limit γ → ∞ in spirit. We keep smooth σ as the default.

---

## What σ is *not* doing here

| You might think… | Actually… |
|------------------|-----------|
| σ decides if *i* gets drafted | No — **top-K on S_i** decides |
| σ outputs a draft probability for *i* | No — it scores **each teammate’s viability**, then we **average** |
| We always binarize at 0.5 | No — we **average** soft values; 0.5 is only the value **at A_j = θ** |
| σ is assignment (ρ) | No — assignment is separate (match to **T_j**) |
| σ is the hero curve | No — hero is **real outcomes**; σ is inside **fake-league score** |

---

## Why this design (dissertation logic)

**Layer B story:** Good peers can help (B) and hurt (D/congestion). **L_C** is the **D-ish congestion measure on the roster** after assignment — “how crowded is my viable-peer field?”

**Layer C (sim):** We need that idea **inside advancement**, not only in prose. So:

- Assignment (ρ) puts you on a roster  
- **σ + θ + γ** define who counts as a viable peer on that roster  
- **L_C** summarizes peer congestion  
- **λ** weights it in **score**  
- **Top-K** picks winners  

The **knockout** on slide 3: same rosters, **λ = 0** vs **λ > 0**. Only difference is whether **L_C** (built with σ) enters **S_i**. That tests “congestion in score matters,” not “sigmoid predicts draft.”

---

## One sentence to keep

**σ turns each teammate’s ability into “how much does this peer count as viable competition?”; L_C averages that over your teammates; λ subtracts that average from your talent in the ranking.**

When you’re ready on sort-and-chop, the θ-straddle team story in memo 06 is exactly “where on the roster σ flips from ≈0 to ≈1 and λ first changes who makes top-K.”

Good — three related but distinct points. Here is the clean version, plus what we added to the deck docs.

---

## 1. Hard vs smooth L_C (documented in slides + walkthrough)

The code builds **both** in `add_loo_pool_columns()`:

| Mode | Config | Per-teammate *j* | **L_C** for player *i* |
|------|--------|------------------|------------------------|
| **Smooth (Phase B deck)** | `crowding_smooth` | σ(γ(A_j − θ)) | LOO **mean** of those weights |
| **Hard (in code, not in deck)** | `crowding` | 1 if A_j > θ else 0 | LOO **share** above θ |

**This deck uses smooth only** (`loo_pool_l_mode="crowding_smooth"` everywhere in Pass B/C and θ/γ diagnostics).

**Updated:**
- Intro slide — **L_C** glossary row + bullet in “How to read this deck”
- Walkthrough — new section **“Hard vs smooth L_C”**
- θ slide auto-builder — `$L_C$ mode: crowding_smooth` note
- Optional figure: `sort_chop_lambda/VIABILITY_hard_vs_smooth.png` (now in `./scripts/build_characterization_slides.sh`)

---

## 2. What would you see with hard L_C?

**Same big story** — λ in score still bends who gets selected. **Different mechanics:**

| | Smooth (what we show) | Hard (counterfactual) |
|---|----------------------|------------------------|
| **γ** | **Matters** — γ sweep slides make sense | **Irrelevant** — only θ; γ sweep would be pointless |
| **Peers near θ** | Graded (~0.5 at A_j = θ) | **Cliff** at θ |
| **L_C values** | Continuous in [0,1] | **Discrete** (0, 1/15, 2/15, …) |
| **λ_crit ≈ 4/γ** | Holds on sort-and-chop (memo 06) | No — sharper cliff; reorder tied to **θ** only |
| **Curve shapes** | Humps, softer transitions | Often **sharper**; same qualitative “congestion bends selection” |

**One-liner if Alex asks:** “Smooth σ is the graded peer-viability story and lets γ be a knob; hard share is the binary limit (γ → ∞). Phase B standardizes on smooth so θ and γ slides hang together.”

The hard-vs-smooth figure shows a θ-straddle roster: soft **L_C ≈ 0.52** vs hard **L_C = 0.43** for the same teammates — same *kind* of interior congestion, different numbers and no γ in the hard case.

---

## 3. Sort-and-chop — your read is basically right

**Yes:** sort-and-chop is **maximum assignment assortativity** — it **removes ambiguity in roster geometry** so γ and λ_crit are easier to characterize.

More precisely:

- **Soft ρ (slides 1–5):** realistic mixing; team talent windows **overlap** (~99% of team pairs overlap on the ability axis). Good for “does assignment matter?” — noisy for “where exactly does λ first reorder ranks?”
- **Sort-and-chop (slides 6–7):** sort all players by **A_i**, chop into equal rosters → **zero between-team overlap**. One **θ-straddle** team, clean **seams** at slice boundaries → λ_crit ≈ 4/γ story is visible.

**Important distinction:** Sort-and-chop is **not** the ρ knob. It **ignores T_j** and is a **hard diagnostic benchmark** (“perfect rank sorting”), not “NCAA-realistic seating.”

**Pairing in the deck:**
- ρ slides → **realistic** assignment world  
- γ / λ_crit slides → **controlled testbed** with extreme, deterministic roster geometry  

Same score rule (**smooth L_C**); different assignment extreme.

---

**Regenerate intro:** `python sports/scripts/build_intro_characterization_slide.py`  
**Re-PDF walkthrough** when ready after your edits.

This is **two code experiments**, bundled because Alex raised both in the same congestion thread. “Behind env flag” = **don’t break the current Phase B deck** while you try PD16 ideas.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**Yes — you can close that editor tab without saving.** That's the right move.

## What SpecStory actually does

**Save AI Chat History** does two things:

1. **Writes the archive** to `.specstory/history/` (timestamped files like `2026-06-11_08-19-11-0400-compass.md`).
2. **Opens a preview** in a new editor tab so you can read the export.

The tab in the editor is a **preview**, not something you need to Save As elsewhere.

## If you click "Don't save" on the unusual line terminators warning

That's fine. SpecStory exports sometimes include Unicode line separators (U+2028 / U+2029). Cursor flags them; they're harmless for the archive.

- **Don't save the preview tab** → nothing extra is written; the copy in `.specstory/history/` is what counts.
- **Do save the preview tab** somewhere like `sports/documents/` → you get a **duplicate** (that's how files like `<!-- Generated by SpecStory, Markdown v2.md` ended up in the repo before).

**Workflow:** Run save → select conversations → OK → **close the preview tab** (Cmd+W). Don't Save is correct.

## Where the history actually lives

```
.specstory/history/
  2026-06-11_08-19-11-0400-compass.md   ← main ongoing archive (updated today)
  2026-05-24_12-52-09-0400-scout.md
  ...
```

That's what git tracks (per your commit rules) and what auto-save updates. To **read** old chats, open files there — not the Untitled preview.

**Quick check after a save:** look in `.specstory/history/` for a file whose timestamp just updated. If it's there, you're done regardless of what you did with the preview tab.

No — there isn’t a separate checklist archive folder today, and that’s intentional.

**Current convention:** superseded checklists stay **in place** under `3-Master_Plan/re_entry/` with dated names:

- `CHARLES_CHECKLIST.md` — live
- `CHARLES_CHECKLIST_archive_20260804_pd15.md`
- `CHARLES_CHECKLIST_archive_20260803.md`

That matches how re-entry was set up: [`PARKED_FOR_LATER.md`](3-Master_Plan/re_entry/PARKED_FOR_LATER.md) says these are **“archived in place”** so you don’t have to hunt another tree. Pointers live in `00_READ_ME_FIRST.md`, the live checklist, and `PARKED_FOR_LATER.md`.

**Other “archive” locations in the repo serve different jobs:**

| Folder | Use |
|--------|-----|
| `3-Master_Plan/obsolete/` | Old agent mail, superseded COMPASS docs — not Charles checklists |
| `sports/archive/` | Retired notebooks |
| `re_entry/HEROs_and_PASSes/.../archive/` | Old sweep CSVs / experiments |

So for checklists, **archive-in-place + `_archive_YYYYMMDD` suffix** is the appropriate pattern, not a subfolder.

If you want a tidier `re_entry/` root, a reasonable addition would be `re_entry/archive/checklists/` with a one-line `README.txt` — but we’d need to **move the two archive files and update links** in `00`, `PARKED`, `CHARLES_CHECKLIST.md`, and `PD15_notes.md`. Worth doing only if clutter bothers you; functionally the current setup is correct.

**Model change #2** is Alex’s way of saying: stop picking θ by hand (like 0.72 from the 539 preset). **Derive it from how selective the league is (K/N) and what the ability distribution looks like.**

---

## The shorthand decoded

**θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)**

Read it in three pieces:

| Piece | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **A** | Player ability (what you draw as **A_i** — Beta(2,2) on [0,1] in the sim, or empirical talent in data) |
| **F_A** | **CDF** of ability: F_A(a) = P(A ≤ a) = “fraction of players at or below ability *a*” |
| **F_A⁻¹** | **Inverse CDF** (quantile function): “what ability level has exactly fraction *p* of the population at or below it?” |
| **K/N** | Selection rate — e.g. K=560 slots, N=5600 players → **10%** advance |
| **1 − K/N** | Fraction that **does not** advance (if K/N advance, then 1−K/N stay below the cutoff) |

So:

**θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)** means:

> Find the ability cutoff where **(1 − K/N)** of players are at or below it — equivalently, **K/N** of players are above it.

That cutoff **is** θ.

---

## Plain-English version (Alex’s “naive draft”)

1. Imagine **no teams**, no congestion, no sigmoid ambiguity — pure talent ranking.
2. Exactly **K/N** of the league gets drafted (top K out of N).
3. Draw the ability curve (PDF). Find cutoff **A\*** so the **area to the right** equals **K/N**:

```text
P(A > A*) = K/N
```

4. Set **θ = A\***.

The sigmoid σ(γ(A_j − θ)) then adds **soft ambiguity around that cliff**, not the cliff itself.

---

## Why “CDF” shows up

The CDF is just the bookkeeping for “what fraction is below this point?”

- **F_A(θ) = P(A ≤ θ) = 1 − K/N**
- Solve for θ → **θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)**

Same idea as: “θ is the **(1−K/N) quantile** of the ability distribution” — e.g. at K/N = 10%, θ is the **90th percentile** of A.

---

## Concrete example (sim default)

Ability draw: **Beta(2,2)** on [0,1].  
K/N = **10%** → 1 − K/N = **0.90**.

In Python:

```python
from scipy.stats import beta
theta = beta.ppf(1 - K/N, 2, 2)   # ≈ 0.68 at 10%
```

Compare to today’s preset **θ = 0.72** — close, but **not tied to K/N**. If K/N = 1% (MBB-like), the quantile θ drops; at 40% (Army-like), it rises. That’s why the θ×K/N grid used fixed {0.50, 0.72, 0.90} before PD16; after PD16, θ **tracks K/N by construction** when `GALLERY_THETA_MODE=k_over_n`.

---

## One-line summary

**θ is the talent level that separates the top K/N of the ability distribution from the rest** — computed from the CDF/quantile, not chosen as a free knob.

If helpful, I can add this decode as a short box in doc **08** or the PD16 notes so you don’t have to re-derive F_A⁻¹ each time.

_**User**_

What would that formula look like hand written or in Latex

---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

## LaTeX

**Cutoff definition (Alex’s whiteboard):**

\[
\mathbb{P}(A_i > \theta) = \frac{K}{N}
\]

**Equivalent CDF form:**

\[
F_A(\theta) = \mathbb{P}(A_i \le \theta) = 1 - \frac{K}{N}
\]

**Quantile / inverse-CDF (the PD16 shorthand):**

\[
\boxed{\theta = F_A^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)}
\]

**With the sigmoid layered on top (what the model actually uses):**

\[
\sigma\!\bigl(\gamma\,(A_j - \theta)\bigr), \qquad \theta = F_A^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)
\]

**Beta(2,2) sim example:**

\[
\theta = F_{\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)}^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)
\]

In code that’s `scipy.stats.beta.ppf(1 - K/N, 2, 2)`.

---

## Handwritten-style (what Alex was drawing)

```text
        f(A)  ▲
              │     ╱╲
              │    ╱  ╲
              │   ╱    ╲____
              │  ╱│←───→│
              └──┴───A*──┴────► A
                  θ = A*

   area to the RIGHT of θ  =  K/N
   area to the LEFT  of θ  =  1 − K/N
```

Or as a one-liner on the margin:

```text
   θ  :=  the ability where  P(A > θ) = K/N
        =  F_A^{-1}(1 − K/N)
```

---

## Copy-paste LaTeX block (for a slide or memo)

```latex
% Naive-draft viability threshold (PD16)
\mathbb{P}(A_i > \theta) = \frac{K}{N}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F_A(\theta) = 1 - \frac{K}{N}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\theta = F_A^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)
```

The middle step is the CDF; the last line is the inverse-CDF / quantile shorthand from the PD16 notes.

## Yes — you already have a config pattern (extend it, don’t fork the codebase)

There are **three layers** today:

| Layer | File | Role today |
|-------|------|------------|
| **Gallery toggles** | `sports/scripts/gallery_knobs.py` | Env vars for characterization runs (`GALLERY_PRESET`, `GALLERY_K_OVER_N`, `GALLERY_RHO_HIGH`, …) |
| **Sim defaults** | `sports/tier1_sim_config.py` | Python constants (`VIABILITY_THETA`, `LOO_POOL_L_MODE = "crowding_smooth"`, …) |
| **539 reference JSON** | `sports/tier1_539_reference_settings.json` | Snapshot values (θ=0.72, λ=0.55) — **not** wired as the single switch for all gallery scripts |

**L_C and θ are computed in** `sports/tier1_pool_assignment.py` — mainly `add_loo_pool_columns()` (LOO crowding) and `assign_selection()` (score uses that L column).

Characterization scripts (`pass_c_rho_ablation_bundle.py`, `theta_oat_diagnostic.py`, etc.) already import `gallery_knobs` for K/N and seed, then read θ from `tier1_sim_config`.

---

## Recommendation: modes in one place, branches in the engine — **no code copy**

**Do not** copy/archive `tier1_pool_assignment.py` and maintain two versions. That gets confusing fast and the decks will drift.

**Do this instead:**

1. **Add two env knobs to `gallery_knobs.py`** (PD16 plan — still the right idea):

   ```bash
   export GALLERY_LC_MODE=loo_smooth      # default — current deck
   export GALLERY_LC_MODE=team_smooth     # PD16 team L_C

   export GALLERY_THETA_MODE=preset       # default — 0.72 from 539
   export GALLERY_THETA_MODE=k_over_n     # θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)
   ```

2. **Add a small resolver** in `gallery_knobs.py` (or next to `AssignmentParams`):

   ```python
   def resolve_viability_theta(k_over_n, ability_dist="beta_2_2") -> float: ...
   def lc_mode_to_pool_l_mode(lc_mode: str) -> tuple[str, str]: ...  # scope + column kind
   ```

3. **Branch once in `tier1_pool_assignment.py`**:
   - **L_C:** `add_loo_pool_columns()` stays as-is; add `add_team_crowding_columns()` (same σ(γ(A−θ)), but **team mean, broadcast to roster** — no LOO).
   - **θ:** if `k_over_n`, compute quantile before building L_C; else use preset from config/JSON.

4. **Default = current behavior.** Unset env vars → regenerate **identical** PNGs to today’s deck. That’s your safety net.

5. **Optional suffix on outputs** when modes differ, e.g. `GALLERY_PASS_C_PNG_SUFFIX=_team_lc` — you already use this pattern for sort-and-chop variants.

**Git is the archive.** Tag or commit message: “Phase B deck baseline (LOO + preset θ).” No need to duplicate files in `sports/archive/` unless you want a frozen notebook — for library code, branches beat copies.

---

## What *not* to do

| Approach | Problem |
|----------|---------|
| New conda env | Wrong layer — this is **shell env vars**, not Python environment |
| Only JSON file toggles | Gallery scripts don’t consistently read JSON today; env + resolver is cleaner |
| Fork whole assignment module | Two bugs fixes, two θ formulas, guaranteed confusion |

---

3. **One script end-to-end** — e.g. `pass_c_rho_ablation_bundle.py` with new modes; compare PNGs side-by-side.
4. **Then** θ(K/N) + re-run θ OAT / θ×K/N diagnostics.
5. **Then** intro slide + doc 07 footer when you’re happy with the diff.

## Comment strategy (my proposal — approve before we code)

### Principle: three layers, not wall-of-text

Your codebase already has good module-level glossaries in `tier1_pool_assignment.py`. PD16 comments should **extend that pattern**, not duplicate doc 07/08 in every function.

| Layer | Where | Purpose | Length |
|-------|--------|---------|--------|
| **A. PD16 banner** | Top of `gallery_knobs.py` + one block in `tier1_pool_assignment.py` | *Why* Aug 2026 changed L_C and θ; pointer to doc 08 | ~15–25 lines once |
| **B. Mode dispatch** | Functions that branch on `LC_MODE` / `THETA_MODE` | *What differs* between `loo_smooth` vs `team_smooth`, `preset` vs `k_over_n` | 3–5 lines per branch |
| **C. Line math** | Inside team-L_C and theta-quantile helpers only | *How* the formula is implemented (LOO subtract self vs team mean; `ppf(1−K/N)`) | 1 line where non-obvious |

**Avoid:** repeating the full naive-draft story in every diagnostic script. Those scripts get **one import-line comment** + footer text on the PNG title, not another essay.

---

### What each file should say (concrete)

Short answer: **No.** Alex did **not** say to compute ρ the same way as θ (no CDF quantile, no “ρ = F⁻¹(1 − K/N)” formula).

---

## What Alex said about ρ (three different things)

### 1. **Interpretation** (immediate — whiteboard Sketch A)

ρ **dials how spread out team L_C is** across the league:

- **Low ρ** → narrow spike (teams look similar in congestion)
- **High ρ** → spread / bimodal (weak teams L_C ≈ 0, strong teams high L_C)

That’s a **story about what ρ does inside the model**, not a formula for picking ρ from data.

**New work:** histogram of # teams vs L_C per ρ arm + 2D heatmap (team ability vs L_C).

### 2. **Characterization tweak** (still OAT, not calibration)

- Low-ρ arm still not flat enough → try **ρ → 0.001**
- One clean **intuition sentence** for why ρ matters in *this* construction

That’s still sensitivity slides, not “derive ρ from a CDF.”

### 3. **Calibration** (later — Phase C)

From the end-of-meeting roadmap:

| Knob | How to pin it |
|------|----------------|
| **θ** | **Quantile:** θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N) — **closed form** from ability draw + selectivity |
| **ρ** | **Match assignment assortativity in data** — empirical fit to how teams/rosters sort in the panel |

So ρ is **data-identified**, like θ, but **not via the same mechanism**. θ comes from a **naive-draft tail cut** on the ability distribution. ρ comes from **matching how assignment works in the data** (assortativity of team formation / roster sorting).

---

## Side-by-side

| | **θ (PD16)** | **ρ (PD16)** |
|---|--------------|--------------|
| **Principled definition?** | Yes — naive draft cutoff | Yes — but **different object** |
| **Formula given?** | P(A > θ) = K/N → θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N) | **No** quantile formula |
| **From what?** | Ability distribution + K/N | **Assignment** assortativity in empirical data |
| **Immediate coding ask** | Implement `k_over_n` theta mode | Team L_C + **L_C-vs-ρ diagnostic** figures |
| **Still a sweep knob?** | Yes, until k_over_n mode lands | **Yes** — OAT ρ arms stay; calibration is later |

---

## Quote to keep in mind

> “Assortativity is this dialing measure of what’s the spread of the L_Cs.”

That’s **interpretation + diagnostic**, not “compute ρ like θ.”

---

## Implication for your `_pd16` work

**In scope now:** team L_C + θ(K/N) → `_pd16` PNGs for ρ/λ/θ slides (same ρ **sweep arms**, new L_C and θ machinery underneath).

**Separate track (ρ):** new **L_C distribution vs ρ** figures (Sketch A) — that’s the ρ-specific PD16 deliverable Alex actually asked for, not a ρ-from-CDF helper.

When you’re ready to implement, we can keep ρ arms as `{0.1, 1, 8, 32}` (plus maybe 0.001) and only change what L_C and θ mean under the hood for the `_pd16` variants.

---

## What Alex actually said about ρ

Three layers, easy to merge by accident:

| Layer | What | Like θ? |
|-------|------|---------|
| **Now (PD16)** | New **diagnostic**: as ρ sweeps, show how **team L_C spreads** (histogram + heatmap) | No — still OAT, ρ = {0.1, 1, 8, …} |
| **Interpretation** | ρ **dials spread of L_C across teams** | No — story about the mechanism |
| **Later (calibration)** | **“Match assignment assortativity in data”** | **Partially** — data-identified, but **no CDF formula** |

θ: closed form — θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N).

ρ: “find the ρ in our **assignment rule** that matches how sorted / overlapping rosters look in **this domain’s panel**.” Estimator **TBD**; not given at PD16.

---

## Yes, you need ρ to **build assignments**

In the sim pipeline:

```text
draw A_i, T_j  →  soft_assign(ρ)  →  rosters  →  compute L_C  →  score  →  select top K
```

ρ lives in **assignment** (who plays with whom), not in the score. Without it you only have sort-and-chop (ρ → ∞ benchmark) or random mixing (ρ → 0).

For **Phase B / `_pd16` work**, you still **pick ρ arms** for sensitivity — same as today. Alex is **not** asking you to estimate ρ from MBB data before generating `_pd16` PNGs.

---

## “Look at empirical data to get ρ?” — what that would mean

**Yes, in Phase C** — per domain, something like:

- How tightly does player ability align with team quality / target **T_j**?
- How much do talent distributions **overlap** across teams vs sort into tiers?
- If you fit the soft-assign kernel exp(−ρ(A−T)²/…), what ρ reproduces observed roster sorting?

That uses **roster / assignment structure** in the panel (530 for MBB, Army unit data, etc.) — **not** the hero curve, and **not** draft outcomes directly.

Doc 02 already says: *“Calibrating ρ to 530 … is **not** the v1 gate”* — parked under Phase C in your checklist.

---

## How that fits a **general cross-domain model**

The dissertation claim is **structural generality**, not **one global number for every knob**.

| Input | Domain-specific? | How it generalizes |
|-------|------------------|--------------------|
| **K/N** | Yes | MBB ~1%, Army ~40%, gallery 10% |
| **A_i distribution** | Yes | Empirical perf or declared draw (Beta in sim) |
| **θ** | Yes (PD16) | **Same rule everywhere:** quantile at 1−K/N on **that domain’s** A distribution |
| **ρ** | Yes | **Same assignment mechanism everywhere:** soft match to T_j — but **ρ̂ differs** by how sorted that domain’s rosters are |
| **γ, λ** | TBD | Structural constants vs domain-specific — still open |

**Analogy:** a gravity model has the same equation everywhere; **G** doesn’t — you calibrate to local data. Here:

- **Same pipeline:** ASSIGN(ρ) → SCORE(λ, L_C) → SELECT(K)
- **Different calibrated inputs** per domain: K/N, A distribution, ρ̂, (later γ̂, λ̂)

θ generalizes via a **rule** (naive-draft quantile).  
ρ generalizes via a **mechanism** (assortative assignment) + **domain-specific fit** (match empirical sorting).

You do **not** need one ρ = 8.0 for Army, MBB, and tenure. You need: *“In each domain, we measure roster assortativity and set ρ accordingly; the L_C-spread story should line up with the diagnostic.”*

---

## What this means for your next coding step

**Do now (`_pd16`):**

- Team L_C + θ(K/N)
- Regenerate ρ/λ/θ slides with `_pd16` suffix (ρ arms unchanged)
- **New** L_C-vs-ρ diagnostic figures (Sketch A)

**Do not block on:**

- Estimating ρ from 530
- Resolving cross-domain ρ in one shot

**Do later (Phase C):**

- Define ρ̂ for MBB (530 rosters)
- Repeat for Army / tenure when those panels are ready
- Check: does calibrated ρ plus team L_C reproduce the **kind** of L_C spread Alex drew?

---

## One sentence to carry

**θ** = same **formula**, different inputs (A, K/N).  
**ρ** = same **assignment rule**, different **fitted strength** per domain from how teams actually sort talent.

If you want, next we can sketch what a minimal ρ̂ from 530 might look like (even as a one-paragraph “Phase C stub”) so Phase C doesn’t feel like a blank — but it shouldn’t gate the `_pd16` implementation.

Good slides — the comparisons tell a coherent story, and nothing looks like a broken pipeline.

## Overall read

**PD16 changes the magnitudes and where peaks land, but not the qualitative claims Phase B was making.** Assignment (ρ) and congestion-in-score (λ) still move the curves the way Alex wanted. Team L_C + θ = F_A⁻¹(1−K/N) mainly **sharpens** those stories at the top bins rather than reversing them.

One caveat: both knobs changed together in `_pd16`, so you cannot yet say “team L_C alone did X.” For Alex, that is probably fine for now — this is “before/after PD16 definition,” not full ablation.

---

## ρ (Pass C) — assortativity still matters, more at the top

| What you see | Interpretation |
|--------------|----------------|
| **ρ = 0.1, 1.0** — noisy, flat-ish, similar before/after | Low mixing still does not produce a strong inverted-U on pool mean. Same message as before. |
| **ρ = 8, 32** — climb starts later; **purple peaks higher** (~0.25 vs ~0.22) and later (bin 14) | High assortativity **bites harder** under team L_C + θ ≈ 0.804. Elite-bin separation between low-ρ and high-ρ is **clearer** in PD16. |
| Low bins still near zero for high ρ | Sort-and-chop-style “weak teams don’t advance” story still there. |

**For Alex:** ρ still dials how much assignment sorting shows up in selection — and with team L_C, the high-ρ arms are **more dramatic** at the top, which fits his “ρ spreads team L_C across the league” intuition (even before you build the histogram diagnostic).

---

## λ (Pass B) — congestion-in-score still bends; λ=0 unchanged = sanity check

| What you see | Interpretation |
|--------------|----------------|
| **λ = 0** (blue) — nearly identical | Correct: no L_C in score → team vs LOO L_C should not matter. Good implementation check. |
| **λ = 0.55** — peak slightly **higher** (~0.19 vs ~0.18) at bin 13 | Baseline congestion arm a bit stronger under PD16 definitions. |
| **λ = 1** — peak shifts from bin **8 → ~10–11**; elite drop still there but later | High λ still compresses/kills the top, but team-level congestion may **delay** where the penalty hits — worth one sentence on the slide footer. |

**For Alex:** Pass A/B knockout logic still holds: λ in the score bends who gets selected; talent-only is monotone.

---

## θ OAT — computed θ is not “just 0.72 with extra steps”

The single **θ = 0.804** curve sits **between** your old 0.72 and 0.90 arms — exactly where a higher, K/N-linked cutline should land.

- Steeper than 0.72, less extreme than 0.90  
- Peak ~bin 13 at ~0.195  

**For Alex:** Preset 0.72 was a reasonable teaching default, but **naive-draft θ at K/N = 10%** is more selective and moves the curve. That supports PD16’s “θ from ability + K/N,” not “keep 0.72 forever.”

---

## θ × K/N — the co-movement story is now built in

| K/N | Computed θ | Peak bin (PD16) |
|-----|------------|-----------------|
| 1% (MBB-like) | ~0.94 | 12 |
| 10% | ~0.80 | 13 |
| 40% | ~0.57 | 16 |

Peak bin **rises with selectivity** when θ tracks K/N — that is the PD16 design working. At 40% K/N you still saturate at bin 16 (everyone-advances-ish regime).

Compared to the old 3×3 grid at “similar θ”: not point-for-point identical (expected — θ is **defined** by K/N now, not free), but the **pattern** is sensible: tighter selection + higher θ at low K/N; looser θ + higher K/N at Army-like rates.

---

## What I would say to Alex in one breath

> “We kept the same assign → score → select pipeline. PD16 only changes **how L_C is measured** (team vs LOO) and **how θ is set** (K/N quantile vs 0.72 preset). The ρ and λ characterization stories still hold; high-ρ and high-λ effects are **stronger at elite bins**. θ = F_A⁻¹(1−K/N) sits between our old OAT arms and co-moves with K/N as intended. Next: L_C-vs-ρ histograms to give ρ a model-internal interpretation.”

---

1. **ρ slide:** “PD16: high ρ peaks later/higher — assortativity + team congestion.”  
2. **λ slide:** “λ = 0 unchanged → confirms toggle; λ > 0 bend shifts with team L_C.”  
3. **θ slide:** “θ = 0.804 = Beta(2,2) quantile at K/N = 10%; not comparable to θ OAT grid — different experiment.”  
4. **θ×K/N:** Label the three points with (K/N, θ) pairs so Alex sees θ tracking explicitly.

## Story for Alex (matches his whiteboard)

**1D — ρ spreads team congestion**
- **Low ρ (0.001–1):** one narrow hump around L_C ≈ 0.15 — teams look alike.
- **High ρ (8):** bimodal — pile at L_C ≈ 0 (weak rosters) + second hump ~0.3–0.45 (elite rosters).

**2D — better teams → more congestion at high ρ**
- Low ρ: tight cloud (ability ~0.5, L_C ~0.15).
- ρ=8, 32: upward tail — high-ability teams drift to high L_C (the diagonal he sketched).

That is the model-internal read: **ρ controls how heterogeneous team congestion is across the league**, not just how the selection curve bends.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Alex wanted the **1D plot** to answer a simple question that Pass C alone does not:

**When assignment gets more assortative (ρ goes up), how does team congestion spread out across the league?**

## What to plot

- **X-axis:** each team’s congestion, **L_C** (team-level: how crowded that roster is)
- **Y-axis:** **how many teams** fall in each L_C bin (a histogram)
- **One panel per ρ arm** (low → high), same league draw, same θ — only assignment changes

No score step, no selection step. Just: assign rosters → compute team L_C → count teams.

## What Alex expected to see

**Low ρ (random-ish matching):**
- Almost all teams land in **one narrow hump**
- Teams look **alike** in congestion — not flat/uniform, but a tight spike
- Plain English: *everyone faces roughly similar peer pressure*

**High ρ (strong sorting):**
- The histogram **spreads out** — often **bimodal**
- **Weak teams** pile up near **L_C ≈ 0** (barely any viable peers)
- **Strong/elite teams** sit at **higher L_C** (lots of good teammates above θ)

Plain English: *ρ controls how heterogeneous congestion is across teams — weak rosters are quiet, elite rosters are crowded.*

## Why Alex cared

Pass C shows “the selection curve moved.” The 1D plot shows **why** in the model:

> **ρ doesn’t just bend the outcome plot — it reshapes the league-wide distribution of team congestion.**

That gives ρ a concrete internal meaning Alex can point to on the whiteboard, separate from “the curve looked different.”

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

You're right — that was a real bug, not just you.

## What was wrong

The old 1D plot used matplotlib's **shared x-axis** across rows. That hides tick numbers on the **top three panels** — only the bottom row showed 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, etc. The only x-label was one cryptic formula squeezed at the very bottom:

*Team smooth L_C = mean σ(γ(A_k−θ))*

So the top panels looked like unlabeled bar charts.

## What the x-axis actually means (plain English)

**X = team congestion L_C** for each roster (350 teams, one value per team):

- **0** → almost no strong peers on that roster (weak/uncompetitive team)
- **~0.15** → moderate peer pressure (typical at low ρ)
- **Higher (0.3–0.6)** → roster is crowded with players above the viability threshold θ

**Y = how many teams** fall in each L_C bin (a histogram).

Each panel is a different **ρ** (how assortative assignment is). You're asking: *"When ρ changes, does congestion spread out across teams?"*

## Fixed PNGs

Regenerated with:
- **0.0–1.0 tick numbers on every panel**
- Plain x-axis label: *"Team congestion L_C (0 = roster has almost no strong peers; 1 = roster is very crowded with strong peers)"*
- Clearer title: *"How many teams at each congestion level?"*

Files updated:
- `pass_c_rho/LC_distribution_vs_rho_1d_pd16.png`
- `pass_c_rho/LC_distribution_vs_rho_2d_pd16.png` (clearer axis labels too)

Refresh the image in your deck (Change Picture) or rebuild slides:

```bash
python sports/scripts/build_lc_congestion_characterization_slide.py
```

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

That confusion makes sense — the numbers look like they should have units, but **L_C doesn't have physical units** (not wins, dollars, or headcount). It's a **model index on a fixed 0→1 scale**.

## What the axes actually are

| Axis | "Unit" | What the numbers mean |
|------|--------|------------------------|
| **X (L_C)** | **Unitless index, 0→1** | How crowded that roster is with strong peers. Built as the average sigmoid viability of teammates near θ. **0 = none**, **1 = maximum**. |
| **Y (1D plot)** | **Teams (count)** | How many of the 350 teams fall in each L_C bin. This one *does* have a unit: headcount. |
| **Y (2D plot, ability)** | **Unitless index, 0→1** | Normalized roster talent (mean ability on [0,1] scale). |
| **Color (2D heatmap)** | **Teams (count)** | How many teams land in each (L_C, ability) cell. |

So when you see **L_C ≈ 0.15**, read it as: *"this team's congestion index is 0.15 on a 0–1 scale"* — roughly low–moderate peer pressure, not "0.15 of something physical."

## Why Alex still uses 0–1

Ability **A** is also on [0,1] in the sim. L_C is derived from how many teammates clear the viability threshold θ, so it naturally lives on **[0, 1]** too. The plot is asking: *where on that index do teams pile up?*

## Updated on the PNGs

- X-axis now says **`[unitless, 0 → 1]`** with **(none)** and **(max)** at the ends  
- Y-axis says **`Number of teams (count)`**  
- Footnote: *"L_C has no physical units — it is a model index bounded between 0 and 1."*

Refresh `LC_distribution_vs_rho_1d_pd16.png` in your viewer — the scale should read much clearer now.

New file ready — open this side-by-side comparison:

**`pass_c_rho/LC_distribution_vs_rho_1d_overlay_pd16.png`**

**Left panel — single hue (blues):** light = low ρ, dark = high ρ. Same story, cleaner for a slide; the dark ρ=32 spike at L_C≈0 pops against the pale low-ρ hump.

**Right panel — multi-color (plasma):** one color per ρ arm. Easier to pick out a specific ρ in the legend; more visual noise where distributions overlap.

Both show the same pattern in one glance:
- Low ρ (purple/pale blue): tight hump ~L_C ≈ 0.15
- High ρ (yellow/dark blue): mass shifts left to L_C ≈ 0, plus a secondary bump at higher L_C

**X-axis:** L_C on both panels. **Legend:** all five ρ values.

For Alex I'd lean **left (blues)** for the main slide — reads as “ρ darkens → distribution spreads left.” Use **right** if you want to point at a specific ρ arm in discussion.

_**User**_

Hmmmm what if we double the number of bins - will that give more smoothing or less?

---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

More bins means **less** smoothing, not more.

A histogram **averages** teams into wide buckets. Fewer, wider bins → counts get pooled → the curve looks **smoother**. More, narrower bins → each bin has fewer teams → the curve gets **spikier** and shows finer detail (plus more sampling noise).

| Bins | Effect |
|------|--------|
| **Fewer** (e.g. 12) | Smoother, chunkier — good for “big picture” |
| **Current** (24) | Middle ground |
| **Double** (48) | Finer detail, more jagged — good for seeing bumps split |

With **350 teams** and **24 bins**, you get ~15 teams per bin on average. At **48 bins**, ~7 per bin — the high-ρ left spike and right hump may stand out more, but random wiggles will too.

For Alex’s story (“narrow hump → spreads out”), **24 is probably fine**; 48 helps if you want to inspect shape details. I can regenerate the overlay at 48 bins side-by-side with 24 if you want to compare visually.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Here’s a deeper read of the **bottom text on the 1D strip slide** — the four bullets plus the bold **Claim** line — in plain language you can use with Alex.

---

## What the slide is doing (context)

This slide is **not** Pass C. You never score or select anyone. You:

1. Draw one league (same talents, same team targets, seed 42)
2. Re-assign rosters at different **ρ**
3. Compute **team L_C** for each of 350 teams
4. Count how many teams fall at each L_C level

So every panel answers: *“If assignment looked like this ρ, how crowded would rosters be?”*

---

## The four bullets (readout band)

### 1. “Read left→right: low ρ = one narrow spike near L_C ≈ 0.15”

**What you’re seeing:** The first three panels (ρ ≈ 0, 0.1, 1) look almost the same — one tight hump around **L_C ≈ 0.15**, peak ~65–70 teams.

**What that means:** When assignment is mostly random (little sorting on ability vs team target), **almost every team faces similar peer pressure**. Weak teams and strong teams get mixed rosters; nobody gets a special “all-stars” or “all-bench” environment.

**Why ≈ 0.15 and not 0:** L_C isn’t “do you have good teammates yes/no.” It’s the average sigmoid viability of the whole roster around θ ≈ 0.804. Even mixed rosters have *some* players near the threshold, so L_C sits in a moderate band — not at zero.

**Alex line:** *“Low ρ → congestion is a league-wide constant, not stratified by team quality.”*

---

### 2. “High ρ = mass at L_C ≈ 0 (weak rosters) + second hump at elite L_C”

**What you’re seeing:** ρ = 8 and especially ρ = 32: a **tall spike at L_C ≈ 0** plus a **broader bump** around 0.3–0.5 (and a tail toward 0.6 at ρ = 32).

**What that means:** Strong assortativity **splits** the league into two kinds of teams:

| Team type | Who’s on the roster | L_C |
|-----------|---------------------|-----|
| **Weak / low-target teams** | Mostly below θ | **Near 0** — almost no “viable” peers |
| **Elite / high-target teams** | Many above θ | **Higher L_C** — roster feels crowded with strong peers |

That’s the **bimodal** story Alex drew on the whiteboard: not one hump that widens — a **pile at zero** plus a **second hump** for elites.

**Why the left spike gets taller at higher ρ:** More sorting → more teams land in genuinely weak environments. At ρ = 32, ~**110 teams** in the lowest bin vs ~65 at low ρ — that’s almost a third of the league in “no peer pressure” rosters.

---

### 3. “No score/select — ASSIGN + team L_C only. Same y-axis across panels.”

Two separate points:

**No score/select:** This isolates **ρ’s effect on roster environments** before asking “who gets promoted?” Pass C shows what happens *after* you score; this shows **what world ρ built**. Alex wanted that separation so ρ isn’t only “the selection curve moved.”

**Same y-axis:** That’s why you insisted on the strip layout. In the old multi-panel grid, each panel auto-scaled and the ρ = 32 spike *looked* similar in height to the low-ρ hump. On a **shared 0–120 scale**, you see the truth: the ρ = 32 spike is **much** taller — a real mass of teams at L_C ≈ 0, not a visual trick.

---

### 4. “At ρ = 32: 48% of teams below L_C = 0.05; left panels ≈ narrow hump at low ρ”

This is the **numbers anchor** for the story:

| ρ | std(L_C) | % teams with L_C &lt; 0.05 |
|---|----------|---------------------------|
| ≈ 0 – 1 | ~0.05 | ~1% |
| 8 | 0.13 | **32%** |
| 32 | 0.16 | **48%** |

**Subtle but important:** **Mean L_C ≈ 0.15 is almost identical across all ρ arms.** Sorting doesn’t change “average congestion” in a simple way — it changes **who** gets which congestion. Variance and tails move; the average is stable. That’s why “ρ spreads the distribution” is more accurate than “ρ raises congestion.”

---

## The footer Claim (the one-liner)

> **Claim:** ρ stratifies team congestion across the league — low-ρ mixing yields one narrow L_C hump; high-ρ assortativity piles weak teams at L_C ≈ 0 and elite rosters at higher L_C. Shared y-scale: compare peaks honestly.

**Unpacking:**

- **“Stratifies”** — ρ creates **heterogeneity** across teams (some low L_C, some high), not one shared experience.
- **“Low-ρ … one narrow hump”** — league looks ** homogeneous** in peer pressure.
- **“Piles weak teams at L_C ≈ 0”** — sorted assignment puts low-talent teams together → no one clears θ → congestion index collapses.
- **“Elite rosters at higher L_C”** — the second hump / tail; preview of the 2D slide.
- **“Shared y-scale”** — methodological honesty for Alex; you’re not cherry-picking axis limits.

---

## How this connects to Pass C (for Alex)

Pass C asks: *given fixed score and top-K, how does the selection-by-pool-mean curve change with ρ?*

Sketch A answers: *because ρ reshaped **who sits in which peer environment** before selection.*

Low ρ → everyone in similar L_C → selection curve stays flat.  
High ρ → elite teams in high-L_C worlds, weak teams in low-L_C worlds → once you **put L_C in the score**, you get the inverted-U / pool-mean story.

**One sentence for the meeting:**  
*“ρ doesn’t just bend the outcome plot — it first decides whether your team is a crowded elite roster or a quiet weak one; the strip shows that split directly.”*

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**Use the whole inverse: \((F_A)^{-1}\)** — not \(F_{A^{-1}}\).

| Notation | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **\(F_A^{-1}(1 - K/N)\)** or **\((F_A)^{-1}(1 - K/N)\)** | **Inverse CDF** (quantile function) of ability \(A\), evaluated at \(1 - K/N\) ✓ |
| **\(F_{A^{-1}}(\ldots)\)** | Looks like “\(F\) subscript \(A^{-1}\)” — **not** standard, easy to misread ✗ |

**Story:** \(F_A\) is the CDF of the ability draw. **θ** is the cutoff where a fraction **\(K/N\)** of the league would advance in the naive-draft thought experiment — so you want the **\(1 - K/N\)** quantile:

\[
\theta = F_A^{-1}(1 - K/N)
\]

**PowerPoint / Equation Editor:** subscript **A** on **F**, then superscript **-1** on the **\(F_A\)** group (not only on A). Or type **(F_A)^-1** explicitly.

**Plain English on the intro slide** (if math is fussy):

> θ = ability cutoff where top K/N of the talent distribution would advance (naive draft)

That matches `gallery_knobs.py` and doc 08 (`F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)`).

|---|---|

| Team **L_C** from sim assignment | Team **L_C** on actual rosters (team-level σ formula) |

Great — this is a clean spec. Here’s a working agreement plus the two things worth deciding together: **pool** and **L_C alternatives**.

---

### Locked (from your list)

| Choice | Recommendation |
|--------|----------------|
| **Unit** | **Team-season** — one row per `(team_id, season)` in the 1D/2D plots |
| **Ability** | **PPM** (align with Pass A hero) |
| **K/N** | Computed from the **same filtered panel** as the plot; report **2 sig figs** (e.g. `K/N = 0.011` or `1.1%`) |
| **L_C** | **Team smooth** — annotate on plot |
| **ρ** | **No sweep** — single empirical league; caption names ρ descriptively |

---

### 1. Pool — what to list on the plot

In the panel code, **“pool” = roster group `(team_id, season)`** — teammates are everyone on that team that season who pass your filters.

Put **two counts** in the subtitle (they answer different questions):

| Label | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **Analysis pool** | Player-seasons after filters → defines **N** and the **θ** CDF |
| **Team-seasons plotted** | Unique `(team_id, season)` → **one** \(L_C\) and **one** team-mean PPM each |

**Suggested plot line:**

> Unit: **team-season** · Pool: `(team_id, season)` rosters · Player-seasons **N = …** · Team-seasons **T = …** · Seasons **2011–2021** · min minutes ≥ 20 · PPM z-within-season

**Pool decision for you:** use the **Pass A hero filters** (2011–2021, min 20 min, ppm z-within-season, poolq winsor 0.01/0.99) so empirical Sketch A matches the hero Alex already knows — or loosen `restrict_teams_by_draftees` and document it. Pass A uses `restrict_teams_by_draftees=False`; say that explicitly if you keep it.

---

### 2. PPM — raw vs z-within-season

Pass A hero uses **PPM → z-within-season** before poolq. For Sketch A:

- **Recommend z-within-season PPM** as \(A_i\) — same ability scale as the hero, era-comparable.
- **θ** = empirical quantile of **all player-seasons’ z-PPM** at \(1 - K/N\) (pooled across seasons in the analysis pool).
- **Team mean A** (2D y-axis) = mean z-PPM on that roster.

Raw PPM is an option later for a “absolute points” appendix; I wouldn’t lead with it.

---

### 3. K/N — how to compute (2 sig figs)

On the **filtered analysis pool**:

\[
K = \sum_i \mathbf{1}[\text{drafted}], \quad N = \text{\# player-seasons}, \quad K/N = K/N
\]

Report e.g. **`K/N = 0.011`** (not `0.0107`). Optionally show `K = …, N = …` in a footnote.

**θ** then: \(\hat\theta = \widehat{F_A^{-1}}(1 - K/N)\) on the z-PPM empirical CDF — list \(\hat\theta\) to 2–3 decimals on the plot.

---

### 4. L_C options — why **team smooth** for this slide

| Mode | Who gets a value | Formula (peers) | Role |
|------|------------------|-----------------|------|
| **team smooth** ✓ | One per **team-season** | mean\(_k \sigma(\gamma(A_k-\theta))\) over **whole roster** | PD16 / Alex: “how crowded is **this team**?” — matches 1D/2D unit |
| **LOO smooth** | One per **player** | LOO mean σ over teammates | Pass A **poolq_loo** hero; fine for **outcome** curves, not team-level Sketch A |
| **LOO hard** | One per player | LOO share with \(A_j > \theta\) | Binary limit; γ sweep / λ_crit geometry |
| **Team hard** | (not wired) | Roster share above θ | Rarely needed; cliff version of team smooth |

**Plot annotation:**

> \(L_C\): **team smooth** — mean\(_k \sigma(\gamma(A_k - \theta))\) on roster · \(\gamma = 10\)

LOO would give **different** \(L_C\) per player on the same team — wrong unit for a team-season histogram.

---

### 5. ρ — no sweep; caption descriptor

Real rosters weren’t generated with soft-ρ arms. Options for **`ρ = [descriptor]`**:

| Descriptor (V1) | Pros |
|-----------------|------|
| **`observed assignment (empirical rosters)`** | Honest; no fake precision |
| **`within-team ability dispersion`** (mean roster SD of z-PPM) | One number; describes spread |
| **`ρ̂`** from a fitted match-to-soft-assign model | Phase C; more work |

For Alex-fast V1: caption like:

> Empirical MBB · θ from K/N quantile on z-PPM · \(L_C\) team smooth · **ρ = observed rosters** (assignment not simulated)

Add a numeric ρ̂ in V2 when you pick an estimator.

---

### What the figures look like (vs sim)

| | Sim Sketch A | Empirical V1 |
|--|--------------|--------------|
| **1D** | 5-panel ρ strip | **One** histogram: # team-seasons vs \(L_C\) |
| **2D** | 5 heatmaps | **One** heatmap: team mean z-PPM vs \(L_C\) |
| **Compare to sim** | Optional side-by-side later | Same layout, different caption |

---

### Decisions I need from you

1. **Filters** — lock to Pass A hero spec (2011–2021, min 20, winsor, etc.)?  
2. **PPM** — confirm **z-within-season** (recommended).  
3. **ρ caption V1** — OK with **“observed rosters”** until ρ̂ exists?

Once you confirm those three, we can implement the empirical script mirroring the sim strip/2D code.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Fixed. The sim A_i / T_j slide was broken by a layout bug in `build_sim_input_distributions_slide.py`.

**Root cause:** `body_top` was already a `Length` in EMU, but the code wrapped it again with `Inches(body_top)`. python-pptx treats that number as *inches*, so the sidebar and figure landed millions of inches off-slide (only the title/subtitle/claim were visible).

**What changed:**
1. **Layout** — pass `Length` objects directly to `add_textbox` and `_add_picture_fitted`; no double `Inches()`.
2. **Bullets** — simplified LaTeX (`\sim`, `\approx` instead of raw `\overline` leakage).
3. **`gallery_mathtext.py`** — added `\sim` and `\approx` to the Greek/symbol map.

**Verified positions** (all on a 13.33×7.5 slide):
- Sidebar: top 1.1″, height 5.44″
- Figure: top 1.96″, height 3.72″ (centered in the body area)
- Claim footer: top 6.62″

`3-Master_Plan/re_entry/HEROs_and_PASSes/slides/auto/CHAR_sim_input_distributions_AUTO.pptx`

- Subscripts misaligned or underlined
- Stray vertical rules between math segments

That fragment is from this bullet:

> Left: Aᵢ ∼ **Beta(2,2) on [0,1] (beta_2_2)** — unimodal…

## How those characters are supposed to render

All plain text — no subscripts, no LaTeX:

| Piece | Meaning | Should look like |
|-------|---------|------------------|
| `Beta(2,2)` | Beta distribution, shape params 2 and 2 | Beta**(2,2)** — normal parens, comma |
| `on [0,1]` | Support on the unit interval | on **[0,1]** |
| `(beta_2_2)` | Internal config tag from the sim code | **(beta_2_2)** — literal underscores |
| `—` | Em dash before “unimodal” | — |

So the full phrase should read:

**Beta(2,2) on [0,1] (beta_2_2) —**

## Why you're seeing `beta_(2_2 )`

PowerPoint is treating `_` as subscript markup in `(beta_2_2)`:

- `beta_` → “beta” + subscript
- `2_` → “2” + subscript  
- `2` → subscript character

That turns the config label `(beta_2_2)` into the garbled **beta<sub>(2<sub>2</sub></sub> )** mess in your screenshot.

**Beta(2,2)** is fine — no underscores. The bug is only the **`(beta_2_2)`** token bleeding math-style subscripts into plain text (often worse when it sits next to Cambria Math runs for Aᵢ and ∼).

## Intended vs. broken

- **Intended:** `…on [0,1] (beta_2_2) —`
- **Broken:** `…[0,1](beta_(2_2 ))-` (underscores → fake subscripts, em dash may look like `-`)

If you want this bullet to render reliably everywhere, the fix is to drop or reword that tag — e.g. `Beta(2,2) on [0,1]` without `(beta_2_2)`, or use a form without underscores like `(beta-2-2)`. I can patch the slide builder if you want.

In `tier1_pool_assignment.py`, `AbilityDraw` is a set of string tokens:

```148:151:sports/tier1_pool_assignment.py
AbilityDraw = Literal[
    "uniform_01",              # A ~ U(0,1) — 539-style unit interval

```

When the code sees `"beta_2_2"`, it runs:


```314:314:sports/tier1_sim_config.py
SELECTION_539_ABILITY_DRAW = "beta_2_2"
```

So **`beta_2_2` = “draw abilities from Beta(2,2) on [0,1]”** — the underscores encode the shape parameters in a JSON/state-friendly way (no commas or parens in the token).

## Bottom line

| Token | Role |
|-------|------|
| `beta_2_2` | Internal config / meta field name |

## What the code actually meant (jargon, not physics)

In `tier1_pool_assignment.py`, **T_j** was written as “team **target**” — one synthetic number per team that soft assignment *aims at* before rosters form. It is **not** “team j’s realized mean roster talent.”

So there are really **three** objects that got blurred:

| Object | Sim | Empirical MBB |
|--------|-----|----------------|
| **Player talent** | Drawn (Beta, etc.) | z-PPM / performance |
| **Team-level summary** | Mean of assigned players on roster j | Mean z-PPM on team-season roster |
| **Assignment attractor** (sim only) | Drawn Uniform[0,1], feeds ρ kernel | *Doesn’t exist* |

If **T = team**, then **T_j** should name the **middle row** (team mean), not the bottom row (assignment attractor). The codebase used **T** for the wrong row — that’s the source of the confusion.

## On **A** not feeling intuitive

Same issue. **A** was Alex/generative shorthand for latent “ability.” In your data world you think in **PPM**, **performance**, **z-scores within season** — nothing about **A** signals that.

So you don’t have to keep **A** for empirical work, or even for slides aimed at Alex, unless you want symbol continuity with \(S_i = A_i - \lambda L_C\) in the generative section.

---

## Notation options if **T = team** and you drop **A**

### Option A — Player **q**, team **T** (my favorite for you)

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **q_i** | Player talent (sim draw or empirical z-PPM) |
| **T_{jt}** | Team j in season t — **mean q on roster** (observed or post-assignment) |
| **μ_j** or **τ_j** | Sim-only assignment attractor (what code now calls `T_j`) |

Score line: \(S_i = q_i - \lambda L_C\).

Empirical: report **\(\hat{q}_i\)** and **\(T_{jt}\)** (hat on player input from data; team mean often needs no hat if it’s literally the roster average).

### Option B — Keep generative symbols, separate empirical lane

| Lane | Player | Team mean | Sim assignment knob |
|------|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| **Sim** | \(A_i\) (Alex legacy) | \(\bar{A}_j\) | **Target** renamed **μ_j** on slides |
| **Empirical** | \(\hat{q}_i\) or \(\widehat{\mathrm{PPM}}_i\) | **\(T_{jt}\)** | — |

Side-by-side figures don’t force the same letter for player talent across lanes.

### Option C — Words on slides, symbols in appendix

Slides: “player z-PPM,” “team-season roster mean.”  
Equations in memo: pick **q** / **T** once and stick to it.

Alex’s hat idea fits **estimated player inputs from data**, not team targets:

- **\(\hat{q}_i\)** — player talent constructed from NCAA stats  
- **\(T_{jt}\)** — team mean is already an observed aggregate (bar optional; **\(\bar{q}_{jt}\)** is equivalent and very clear)

I would **not** use **\(\hat{T}_j\)** for the sim assignment attractor — that object isn’t estimated from data; it’s invented.

1. **T should mean team-level**, i.e. roster mean **\(T_{jt}\)** in empirical Sketch A.

## Recommended notation (fits your A / T rules)

Use **plain T for the real thing** (what you plot). Give the sim-only draw a **modifier**:

| Symbol | How it looks | Meaning |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| **Tⱼ** | T sub j | **Realized team talent** — average **Aᵢ** on team *j*’s roster |
| **Tⱼₜ** | T sub j, sub t | Same, for team *j* in season *t* (empirical unit) |
| **Tⱼ\* ** or **Tⱼ (tgt)** | T sub j with asterisk, or “tgt” tag | **Sim team target** — pre-assignment draw for soft assign |

**Rule of thumb:**  
- **Y-axis on 2D heatmap** → **Tⱼ** (realized), sim or empirical  
- **ρ assignment equation** → **Aᵢ** matched to **Tⱼ\*** (target)  
- **Empirical deck** → never show **Tⱼ\***; only **Tⱼₜ** from data  

Hat stays for **empirical player** **Âᵢ**, not for sim targets.

---

## Why not two plain T’s?

Both are “team” quantities, but:

- **Target** = input to **ASSIGN** (synthetic knob)  
- **Realized T** = output of **ASSIGN** (what the roster actually looks like)

At high ρ they align; at low ρ they can diverge a lot. That’s the scientific point.

---

## One-line glossary add

> **Tⱼ\*** — sim assignment target (drawn). **Tⱼ** — realized team talent (roster mean of **Aᵢ**). Empirical: **Tⱼₜ** only (no \*).

---

## Slide wording examples

- Sim ρ slide: “Soft assign: match **Aᵢ** to **Tⱼ\***”  
- Sim Sketch A 2D: “**y**: realized **Tⱼ** vs **x**: team **L_C**”  
- Empirical Sketch A: “**y**: **Tⱼₜ** (team-season roster mean of **Âᵢ**); observed rosters”

If you’d rather avoid the asterisk, **Tⱼ (target)** vs **Tⱼ (realized)** in words on the slide, with **Tⱼ\*** only in the glossary, works too. The important part is **never using mean A on the axis** — always **T** for realized team talent.

---

import re
from pathlib import Path
from pptx import Presentation

deck = Path(&#34;3-Master_Plan/re_entry/HEROs_and_PASSes/slides/CHAR_Phase_B_characterization_HAND.pptx&#34;)
prs = Presentation(str(deck))

# patterns to flag
patterns = [
    (re.compile(r&#34;team mean\s*A|mean A on|team mean ability|Team mean A&#34;, re.I), &#34;team-mean-A → use T_j (realized)&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;team talent target|team target|T.sub.j(?!\\*)|T_j(?!\\*|\w)&#34;, re.I), &#34;bare T_j in ASSIGN context → check T_j* vs T_j&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;target T&#34;, re.I), &#34;target wording → T_j*&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;\\beta_2_2|beta_2_2&#34;, re.I), &#34;config tag (optional remove)&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;mean \\?A|mean A[^_]&#34;, re.I), &#34;mean A phrasing&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;A_i.*T_j|T_j.*A_i&#34;, re.I), &#34;A/T pair — verify * on target&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;0\.72&#34;, re.I), &#34;old θ preset? (PD16 uses K/N quantile)&#34;),
    (re.compile(r&#34;team ability&#34;, re.I), &#34;team ability → T_j&#34;),
]

for i, slide in enumerate(prs.slides, 1):
    chunks = []
    for sh in slide.shapes:

        if sh.shape_type == MSO_SHAPE_TYPE.GROUP:

Hey I know this could be a huge pain in the ass but do you think it would look better and make more sense to put the * beside the j in the subscipt instead of back up on the main level after the entire term?

---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes — for slides, **putting the ∗ with the j in the subscript usually looks cleaner and reads better**.

## Two layouts

| Style | Looks like | Reads as |
|--------|------------|----------|
| **A (what you have now)** | T<sub>j</sub>* — star at main line | “T-sub-j, starred” |
| **B (what you’re suggesting)** | T<sub>j∗</sub> — star inside subscript | “T-sub-(j-star)” |

## Why B is often better on your deck

1. **Visual** — The ∗ stays tied to **j** (team index), not floating after the whole symbol. That matches the meaning: the **team slot** is the special “target” draw, not a separate main-level modifier.

2. **Consistency with plain T<sub>j</sub>** — Realized team talent stays **T<sub>j</sub>**; sim target is **T<sub>j∗</sub>**. Same base letter, same index; only the subscript picks up the ∗.

3. **PowerPoint** — In Equation Editor: **T**, subscript **j∗** (or `j*` in the subscript box). Often less awkward than a free ∗ after the equation.

4. **Contrast with Â<sub>i</sub>** — Hat on **A** marks “empirical player”; ∗ on **j** marks “sim assignment team index.” Different markers, different levels — good.

## Semantics (both are fine)

- **T<sub>j</sub>*** ≈ “the object T_j, starred variant”
- **T<sub>j∗</sub>** ≈ “team j’s target slot” (latent / pre-assign)

For Alex, **B** matches your story a bit better: **T∗ is still team-level T**, with the target distinguished in the subscript.

## Recommendation

**Use T<sub>j∗</sub> for sim assignment targets** everywhere you show math (slide 2, ρ ASSIGN line, glossary, intro table).

Keep:
- **T<sub>j</sub>** — realized roster talent (no ∗)
- **T<sub>jt</sub>** — empirical team-season
- **A<sub>i</sub>** / **Â<sub>i</sub>** — unchanged

## LaTeX / code (when you care)

- Display: `T_{j^*}` or `T_{j*}` (star in subscript with j)
- Avoid `T^*_j` (star on T) — that suggests “starred T”, not “target team j”

No rush to change scripts for this — it’s mostly **hand-slide Equation Editor** and glossary wording. If you adopt **T<sub>j∗</sub>**, we can align auto-deck strings and figure titles (`$T_{j^*}$`) in a later pass.

**Bottom line:** Yes — ∗ beside j in the subscript is a good call for your deck; it’s clearer and usually looks more professional than **T<sub>j</sub>***.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**Short answer:** Yes, PowerPoint can do this — but only if pictures are **linked**, not **embedded**. Your current setup (hand deck + `python-pptx` auto decks) **embeds** images, so re-running the build script does **not** update slides that already exist.

## Linked vs embedded

| Mode | What happens when you regenerate `PASS_C_...png` |
|------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Embedded** (default) | Nothing — slide keeps the old bytes baked in |
| **Linked** | Opening the deck (or **Update Links**) pulls the new PNG from disk |

Your auto-deck scripts use `add_picture(...)`, which **always embeds**. The hand deck is the same unless you explicitly linked when inserting.

## How to link in PowerPoint (hand deck)

**Mac (Office 365):**
1. **Insert → Pictures → Picture from File…**
2. Select the PNG under `HEROs_and_PASSes/…`
3. Look for **“Link to File”** (wording varies by version; sometimes under a dropdown or “Insert and Link”)
4. After regenerating figures: open the deck → **Edit → Links → Update Links** (or close/reopen — behavior varies)

**Windows:** same idea — **Insert Picture** with **Link to File** checked; then **File → Info → Edit Links to Files → Update Now**.

**Tip:** keep the `.pptx` and PNGs in **fixed relative paths** (e.g. deck in `slides/`, PNGs in `pass_c_rho/`). Moving the folder or presenting on a laptop without those files breaks links.

## Why we didn’t build it this way

Linked decks are fragile for your workflow:

- **Dropbox paths** can differ across machines
- **Email / USB / Army laptop** — linked PNGs often aren’t there
- **python-pptx** doesn’t reliably support “insert linked picture” for generated decks
- One broken link → empty box on slide 2 in front of Alex

That’s why the checklist says: regenerate PNGs → **Change Picture** in the hand deck (safe embed, you control layout).

## Practical options for you

1. **Status quo (recommended for HAND deck):** `./scripts/build_characterization_slides.sh --pd16` → Change Picture on the few slides that changed. Most stable for presenting.

2. **Linked hand deck (OK if deck + gallery stay on one machine):** link once in PowerPoint; after each figure refresh, **Update Links**. Good for iteration at your desk; risky for travel.

3. **AUTO deck as disposable mirror:** `./scripts/build_characterization_slides.sh --pd16 --auto-slides` rebuilds `slides/auto/CHAR_Phase_B_characterization_AUTO.pptx` with fresh embeds. Compare/copy equation layout from HAND; don’t treat AUTO as the master for typography.

4. **Future automation (if you want):** a small script could open `CHAR_Phase_B_characterization_HAND.pptx` and re-embed named PNGs from fixed gallery paths — same result as Change Picture, no manual clicking, still portable. Say the word if you want that.

**Bottom line:** automatic refresh **is possible** with linked pictures in PowerPoint, but your repo’s generated decks don’t do it today, and for the Alex hand deck, **embedded + Change Picture** (or a refresh script later) is usually the safer call.

### What “sign-off” means (it’s not “rebuild the PNG”)

Alex already **accepted the sort-and-chop rationale** on PD16. Sign-off means **you** can defend three claims without reading the slide:

1. **Why sort-and-chop here?**  
   Not because NCAA assigns that way — because it **removes assignment ambiguity** so γ and λ_crit are readable. Soft ρ slides 1–5 = realistic seating; slides 13–14 = **controlled testbed**.

2. **Why λ = 0 and λ = 0.25 look identical?**

3. **What γ does:**  
   Sharper sigmoid → congestion “turns on” at **lower λ** → inverted-U appears at smaller λ_crit.

**Python default:** `0.001` (used when the env var isn’t set).

**Shell override:** `scripts/rebuild_hero_gallery.sh` line 44 still exports `GALLERY_RHO_LOW` default **`0.1`** before running the gallery rebuild — so if you use that script without overriding env, you get 0.1, not 0.001. `./scripts/build_characterization_slides.sh --pd16` does **not** set it, so it uses the Python default (0.001).

---

## Two different projects Alex has been talking about

Alex has been looking at **two decks** that answer **two different questions**:

| | **Phase B deck (what he just saw)** | **Real-data work (what he's asking for now)** |
|---|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| **Question** | “If I turn knob ρ, λ, θ, γ in a **fake league**, what moves?” | “What does the **actual NCAA panel** look like, and can we **pin ρ and θ from data**?” |
| **Data** | Simulated players, synthetic assignment | MBB 2011–2021 panel (`player_season_panel_530.csv`) |
| **Status** | Built — he saw the hand deck | **Partially built** — hero exists; ρ/θ calibration not yet |

When he says “real data plots ASAP,” he is **not** asking for more sim sweeps. He is asking you to move from **“we characterized the model in sim”** to **“here is what the data say, and here is how we set ρ and θ.”**

Your instinct — **empirically calculate ρ and θ** — is exactly where PD16 pointed for Phase C. But there are **two sub-steps** inside that, and Alex may want both, in order.

---

## Layer 1: The empirical **phenomenon** (already built)

This is **Pass A** — what you have open right now:

- **Left panel:** Draft rate rises monotonically with **own talent** (ppm z within season).
- **Right panel:** Same players, binned on **poolq_loo** (leave-one-out teammate quality) → **inverted-U** at the top.

That plot does **not** estimate ρ or θ. It is the **stylized fact** the whole model is trying to explain: *context matters for who gets drafted, beyond own ability.*

Alex may or may not have seen this in the sim briefing (it was **not** in the Phase B hand deck). If he hasn't, showing it is still worth doing — but it is **Layer A**, not calibration.

---

## Layer 2: Empirical **structure** plots (partially built, not packaged)

Before you “calculate ρ,” Alex wants to **see** that real rosters have the **same kind of structure** the sim deck claimed ρ controls. That is what his **whiteboard Sketch A** was about:

### In sim (slides 15–16 — he saw this)
- **1D:** Histogram of team **L_C** at low ρ vs high ρ → low ρ = narrow spike; high ρ = spread out.
- **2D:** Heatmap of **T_j** (realized roster talent) vs **L_C** (team congestion) → upward cloud at high ρ.

### On real data (not built yet)
Same **shape** of question, but on actual `(team_id, season)` rows:

> “Do better teams actually have more congestion? How spread out is team-level peer pressure across the league?”

That is **not** ρ itself — it is the **empirical picture** ρ is supposed to reproduce once you calibrate. Alex drew this on the whiteboard and said: *“This gives ρ a model-internal interpretation.”*

So when I asked you “hero pair **or** Sketch A on data?” I was really asking:

- **Option A (hero pair):** Show the **player-level outcome** curve (draft rate vs poolq_loo). Answers: *“What pattern are we explaining?”*
- **Option B (Sketch A on data):** Show the **team-level roster structure** (T_jt vs team congestion). Answers: *“What does real assignment/congestion geometry look like before we pick a ρ?”*

Alex probably wants **both**, but **B** is the one that directly parallels what he just saw in sim and sets up ρ calibration.

---

## Layer 3: Empirically **calculate θ and ρ** (what you're asking about — correct, but not done)

This is the **calibration roadmap** from doc 08 — Phase C. Alex explicitly listed which knobs come from data:

| Knob | From data? | How (PD16) | Built? |
|------|------------|------------|--------|
| **A_i** | Yes | Empirical perf distribution | Partially (panel exists) |
| **K/N** | Yes | Domain fact (~1% NBA draft rate for MBB; 10% in gallery sim) | Conceptual only |
| **θ** | Yes | **θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)** — ability quantile at the naive-draft cutoff | **Sim only** (`GALLERY_THETA_MODE=k_over_n`); **not yet on real perf** |
| **ρ** | Yes | **Match assignment assortativity in the panel** | **Not built** |
| **γ, λ** | Open | Principled fit — **not** “slide sim until it matches hero” | Not built |

So yes: Alex wants you to **pin θ and ρ from data**. But that is **not the same as** the hero inverted-U plot. Those are **calibration readouts** — numbers (and maybe small diagnostic figures) that tell the sim what to use.

---

## What θ from data actually means

**θ** is the **viability cutline** in the sigmoid: “Who counts as a viable peer for congestion?”

Alex’s PD16 definition (whiteboard B):

1. Imagine **no teams** — everyone competes on talent alone.
2. Exactly fraction **K/N** of the league gets “selected” (naive draft).
3. Find the ability cutoff **A\*** where the top **K/N** tail of the talent distribution lives.
4. **Set θ = A\*.**

In symbols: **θ = F_A⁻¹(1 − K/N)** — the quantile of the **empirical ability distribution** at rank (1 − K/N).

**Example:** If K/N = 1% (roughly NBA draft rate from college), θ is the **99th percentile** of college perf in your panel. If K/N = 10% (gallery default), θ is the **90th percentile**.

**What you'd deliver to Alex:**
- A number: “On MBB 2011–2021, with K/N = X%, θ_empirical = Y.”
- Maybe a small figure: ability histogram with a vertical line at θ.

**Important:** You already implemented this **in sim** (naive-draft θ mode). Alex now wants the **same logic on real Â_i**, not Beta(2,2).

---

## What ρ from data actually means

**ρ** in the sim is a **dial in the assignment formula** — how sharply players get matched to team targets:

\[
\pi_{ij} \propto \exp\left(-\rho \cdot \frac{(A_i - T_{j^*})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\]

- **Low ρ** → rosters mix; team L_C values cluster together (narrow histogram).
- **High ρ** → strong sorting; weak teams low L_C, elite teams high L_C (spread histogram + upward T_j vs L_C cloud).

**Real college rosters don't have a ρ parameter.** You cannot read ρ off a CSV column. You need an **estimator** that captures “how assortative is roster formation in the panel?”

PD16 says: **“Match assignment assortativity in panel.”** Concretely, that likely means one or more of:

1. **Overlap forensics (530 CELL 8):** Real team talent windows overlap massively; sort-and-chop gives overlap ≈ 1. Real data look like **moderate ρ**, not chop.
2. **Correlation / regression:** How strongly does a player's ability predict their team's mean ability?
3. **Distribution match:** Compare empirical team **L_C** histogram + **T_j vs L_C** heatmap to sim at candidate ρ values; pick ρ that best matches.

**What you'd deliver to Alex:**
- A number: “ρ_empirical ≈ Z” (with a sentence on the estimator).
- Diagnostic plots: empirical Sketch A **plus** maybe sim at ρ_empirical for comparison.

This is **harder than θ** — θ is a clean quantile; ρ requires choosing and defending an estimator.

---

## What γ and λ are *not* (yet)

Alex was explicit: **γ and λ stay free for now.** Do **not** define them as “whatever makes the sim hero match the empirical hero.”

Once ρ and θ are pinned from data, **then** you need principled estimators for γ (sigmoid sharpness) and λ (congestion weight in score). That is later.

---

## So what is Alex actually asking for “ASAP”?

Putting it together, “real data plots ASAP” most likely means a **short empirical package**, not one plot:

### Immediate (show / confirm)
1. **Pass A hero pair** — talent monotone vs poolq_loo inverted-U (exists; may be news to him if sim deck was all he saw).

### Next (structure — motivates ρ)
2. **Empirical Sketch A** — team-season heatmap: **T_jt** vs team congestion on real rosters (mirrors his whiteboard; **not built**).

### Then (calibration — what you're asking about)
3. **θ from data** — quantile of empirical perf at 1 − K/N; report the number (+ optional histogram).
4. **ρ from data** — assortativity/overlap estimator; report the number (+ compare empirical vs sim L_C distribution).

That sequence matches PD16: characterize data → pin identifiable knobs → fit γ, λ later.

---

## The scoping question, explained plainly

When I asked:

> “Hero pair first, or Sketch A on real rosters?”

I was trying to learn **which gap Alex feels most urgently**:

| If he says… | He means… | We do… |
|-------------|-----------|--------|
| **“Show me the hero / inverted-U on real data”** | He wants the **outcome fact** (Layer 1) | Pass A PNG + maybe scout heterogeneity plots |
| **“Show me team congestion vs talent on real rosters”** | He wants **structural evidence for ρ** (Layer 2) | Build empirical Sketch A script |
| **“What are ρ and θ in the data?”** | He wants **calibration numbers** (Layer 3) | θ quantile + ρ estimator — may need Layers 1–2 as supporting figures |

Your read — **he wants ρ and θ calculated empirically** — is the **Layer 3** ask, and it is **correct for the arc**. The “ASAP” part probably still needs **Layer 1–2 plots as supporting evidence** before the numbers land credibly.

---

## Practical question to ask Alex (one sentence)

> “For real data ASAP — do you want the **hero inverted-U** and **team-level T vs congestion** plots first, or do you want us to jump straight to **reporting empirical θ and ρ** with whatever estimator we pick?”

That tells you whether to prioritize **figures** or **calibration memo** this week.

---

## Bottom line for you

- **Yes**, Alex wants **θ and ρ from data** — that is the PD16 calibration path.
- **No**, that is not the same as the Pass A hero plot you have open; the hero is the **phenomenon**, ρ/θ are **inputs to the generative model**.
- **Sim deck = Phase B done.** **Real data = Phase C starting:** hero (done) → empirical Sketch A (next figure) → θ quantile + ρ estimator (next numbers) → γ, λ later.

If you want, I can draft a one-page “Empirical calibration plan” for Alex that lists exactly those four deliverables with proposed estimators for ρ and θ — so you can confirm with him before we build.
